📚 Reference Links

  • The protocol suite, top level — RFC 8825: Overview — Real-Time Protocols for Browser-Based Applications

  • The browser API — W3C: WebRTC — Real-Time Communication in Browsers

  • Encryption is not optional — RFC 8827: WebRTC Security Architecture

  • Media transport and RTP usage — RFC 8834: Media Transport and Use of RTP in WebRTC

  • The codec you will actually ship — RFC 6716: Definition of the Opus Audio Codec

  • Bonus — the open book, and the best single source in this area: WebRTC for the Curious

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The three things the browser gives you? Media capture, a peer connection with NAT traversal, and a data channel.
The one thing it does not define? Signaling — you build it, usually over WebSocket.
Can WebRTC media be unencrypted? No. SRTP is mandatory; plaintext RTP is forbidden.
Typical Opus frame size on the wire? 20 ms (the codec allows 2.5–60 ms).
Is production WebRTC actually peer-to-peer? Rarely past two participants — an SFU sits in the middle.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

WebRTC is the browser's built-in stack for real-time audio, video and arbitrary data with sub-second latency and no plugin. It bundles three things that are otherwise painful: capturing a microphone or camera, punching through NAT to reach another endpoint, and moving media over UDP with its own congestion control and loss recovery. Encryption is mandatory — SRTP keyed by DTLS, no plaintext option. The part people underestimate is that it deliberately leaves signaling out of the spec, so the first thing you build is the piece that gets the two sides talking.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

What does the browser hand you, and what do you still have to build?

You get three APIs and a transport. getUserMedia captures the microphone and camera behind a permission prompt and a secure-context requirement. RTCPeerConnection is the real machinery: it gathers ICE candidates, runs connectivity checks, performs the DTLS handshake, keys SRTP, and then carries RTP with congestion control, retransmission and bandwidth estimation built in. RTCDataChannel gives you SCTP over that same DTLS association for non-media bytes, with tunable reliability.

What you build is everything around the media plane. Signaling is not specified at all, so the exchange of offers, answers and ICE candidates rides on transport you choose. Identity, presence, room membership, authorization, recording, and anything involving more than two participants are yours. That division is the whole shape of a WebRTC system: the hard real-time parts are solved for you, and the ordinary distributed-systems parts are not.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

When is WebRTC the wrong tool, and what would you use instead?

🎯 Really testing: whether you pick by latency requirement rather than by "it does video" — most video problems are not real-time problems.

The dividing line is interactivity. WebRTC buys you sub-second glass-to-glass latency by accepting lossy delivery, per-stream congestion control and a stateful connection per participant; that is worth the complexity only when someone is waiting to respond. Conversation, remote control, live collaboration and voice agents qualify. One-to-many broadcast does not: for a stream nobody talks back to, low-latency HLS or DASH over an ordinary CDN gives you a few seconds of latency, caching, trivial scale and no per-viewer connection state.

The second wrong-tool case is data. WebRTC data channels are excellent when you already have a peer connection and want to avoid a server round trip, but standing up ICE, STUN, TURN and signaling purely to move JSON between a client and your own backend is unjustifiable — that is a WebSocket. My rule is that WebRTC earns its complexity when the media path must not go through your server, or when the latency budget is tight enough that a server hop matters. Otherwise the simpler transport wins.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What runs out first as a session grows from 2 participants to 50?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard failure of any product that ships a mesh prototype and then adds a group feature.

Client uplink and CPU run out first, and they run out quadratically. In a full mesh each participant holds a connection to every other, encoding and uploading its own stream n-1 times; at four participants that is three simultaneous encodes plus three uploads on a laptop already decoding three streams. Session connections grow as n(n-1)/2, so the interesting number is not server capacity — there is no server — but the weakest participant's uplink.

It presents as asymmetric degradation, which is what makes it confusing. The person on the poor connection is not the one who reports it; everyone else sees their video freeze while their own call looks fine. Bandwidth estimation reacts per connection, so one bad path can cause a sender to reduce quality on links that were healthy. The fix is topological, not tuning: an SFU makes each client upload once and download n-1, converting a client-side quadratic into a server-side cost you can provision.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the media path for a product with 1:1 calls, occasional 20-person rooms, and a voice-AI agent that can join any call.

🎯 Really testing: whether you pick one topology and defend it, or bolt three together and inherit all their failure modes.

Start from the highest-stakes constraint: the agent joins arbitrary calls, and a model does not run in a browser. That alone means media must reach a server, which settles the topology argument before it starts — put an SFU in the path for every session including 1:1, rather than running peer-to-peer for two and switching at three. Mode switching sounds like an optimisation and is actually two products: two sets of failure modes, two recording paths, two debugging stories, and a transition that fires exactly when a call is getting busier.

The path is then uniform. Browser to the nearest SFU edge over WebRTC; the SFU forwards selected streams to other participants and feeds a downmixed or per-speaker track to the agent worker, which runs recognition, the model and synthesis and publishes its reply back into the room like any other participant. Signaling is a separate WebSocket service holding room state, and TURN sits beside the SFU for clients that cannot reach it directly. The one place I would keep peer-to-peer is data channels for cursor and control traffic, where a server hop is pure latency.

The failure I would monitor first is relay share — the fraction of sessions whose selected pair is relayed. It predicts both the bandwidth bill and the latency floor, and it moves without warning when a large customer changes a firewall rule. Second is per-participant loss and round-trip time from the SFU's own statistics, which tell you whether a bad experience is the client's problem or yours.

4. Quick Comparison Table

WebRTC WebSocket Low-latency HLS/DASH When you'd actually pick it
Latency Sub-second Sub-second 2–10 s WebRTC or WS when someone responds; HLS when nobody does
Transport UDP (DTLS/SRTP), TCP fallback via TURN TCP TCP over HTTP WebRTC survives loss; TCP stacks stall on it
Loss behaviour Conceals, retransmits selectively Head-of-line blocks Buffers Real-time audio must degrade, not wait
Media handling Capture, codecs, jitter, bandwidth estimation built in You build all of it Player handles it Raw audio over WS means writing your own pipeline
Scale model Per-participant connection state Per-connection state CDN-cacheable Broadcast to thousands is a CDN problem
Infrastructure Signaling + STUN + TURN + usually an SFU A server A CDN The honest cost of WebRTC is four services, not one

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The exchange has three phases and it is worth naming them separately, because they fail differently. Signaling moves two SDP blobs and a stream of ICE candidates through infrastructure WebRTC knows nothing about; if it breaks, nothing starts. Connectivity establishment is ICE — both sides gather candidates, probe pairs with STUN, and nominate one; if it breaks, you get a connection stuck in checking that eventually goes failed. The media plane is DTLS-keyed SRTP over the nominated pair; once it is up, the signaling server can disappear entirely and the call continues.

Where the real math lives is the latency budget, and it is additive. A conversational target of roughly 200–300 ms mouth-to-ear has to absorb capture and encode, network transit, jitter buffer, decode and playback. Opus at a 20 ms frame contributes its frame time plus algorithmic delay, which RFC 6716 puts between 5 ms and 65.2 ms depending on configuration. The jitter buffer is usually the largest single term you control, because it is deliberately trading latency for smoothness — and it is adaptive, so a lossy path silently spends your budget. Every server hop you add is a real addition to this sum, which is why "put the SFU near the user" is a latency decision, not a cost one.

The second piece of arithmetic is the topology cost. In a mesh of n participants each client maintains n-1 connections and the session holds n(n-1)/2; uplink scales with n-1 per client. With an SFU each client uploads once and downloads n-1, so client uplink is constant and the server carries n in and n(n-1) out. That asymmetry is the entire argument for a media server: it moves a quadratic from the weakest device in the call to hardware you can size.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable is time from speech to response, and WebRTC is usually the only part of that budget you can still buy back once the model is chosen. In a voice agent the model's own latency is largely fixed; transport, jitter buffering and the number of hops between the microphone and the inference process are not. Teams that ship audio over a WebSocket to a distant region routinely discover several hundred milliseconds sitting in transport and buffering, and no amount of prompt work recovers it.

It also matters as a cost signal. Relay share — the fraction of sessions that fall back to a TURN relay — sets both the bandwidth bill and the latency floor, and it is driven by your users' networks rather than by your code. It is the number to have on a dashboard before you need it.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

// Minimum viable peer connection. The three APIs, in the order you use them.
const pc = new RTCPeerConnection({
  iceServers: [
    { urls: "stun:stun.example.net:3478" },                  // reflexive candidates only
    { urls: "turn:turn.example.net:3478", username: u, credential: c }, // relay fallback
  ],
  iceTransportPolicy: "all",       // "relay" forces TURN — use it to test the relay path
});

const stream = await navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ audio: true, video: false });
stream.getTracks().forEach((t) => pc.addTrack(t, stream));   // must precede createOffer

pc.onicecandidate = (e) => e.candidate && signal.send({ candidate: e.candidate });
pc.ontrack = (e) => (remoteAudio.srcObject = e.streams[0]);
pc.onconnectionstatechange = () => log(pc.connectionState); // new→connecting→connected→failed

await pc.setLocalDescription(await pc.createOffer());
signal.send({ sdp: pc.localDescription });                   // signaling is yours, not WebRTC's

iceTransportPolicy: "relay" is the single most useful flag here: it forces every candidate through TURN, which is how you test the fallback path deliberately instead of discovering it is broken when a customer's firewall discovers it for you.

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Same peer connection as Section 8, one 1:1 audio call on a typical residential network.

📥 [0] getUserMedia resolves after user grants permission        t = 0 ms
    │
    ▼
🔍 [1] Candidate gathering: host candidate immediately,
        server-reflexive after one STUN round trip (~30 ms),
        relayed after TURN Allocate (~60 ms)                     t ≈ 60 ms
    │
    ▼
📡 [2] Offer posted to signaling, answer returns                 t ≈ 120 ms
        candidates trickle in parallel — not serialised after SDP
    │
    ▼
🔗 [3] STUN connectivity checks on candidate pairs;
        host↔srflx pair succeeds, srflx pair nominated           t ≈ 180 ms
    │
    ▼
🔒 [4] DTLS handshake over the nominated pair, SRTP keyed        t ≈ 240 ms
    │
    ▼
🎯 [5] First SRTP packet; Opus 20 ms frames, jitter buffer
        settles ~40–60 ms of hold                                first audio ≈ 300 ms

  1. Permission is unbounded wall-clock time you do not control, which is why production apps warm the peer connection and gather candidates before the user commits to joining.

  2. Gathering is parallel, and trickle ICE is why the total is not a sum. Vanilla ICE waits for gathering to finish; trickle sends each candidate as it appears, so checks start on early candidates while the TURN allocation — slowest to arrive, and the one you hope not to need — is still in flight.

  3. Signaling latency is entirely yours. The two SDP round trips cross your WebSocket to your server, so a badly placed signaling service adds directly to join time, and no WebRTC tuning improves that segment.

  4. Nomination picks by priority, not by arrival speed — host, then peer-reflexive, then server-reflexive, then relayed — so a working relayed pair loses to a working reflexive pair even if the relay answered first.

  5. The jitter buffer is the last term and the adaptive one. It holds packets to smooth arrival variance, so a lossy path grows it and spends budget silently. On a voice-agent path this is what quietly ruins a mouth-to-ear target nobody is measuring end to end.

10. When TO Use This

When latency is conversational and the media path is bidirectional — calls, live collaboration, remote control, voice agents. Anything where a person is waiting to respond to what they just heard.

When the media must not pass through your servers — privacy-sensitive 1:1 media, or a product where per-stream server bandwidth would dominate unit economics. A genuine advantage, and it evaporates the moment you add an SFU.

When a browser must send audio or video at all without an install. The capture, codec, jitter and bandwidth-estimation machinery is the hardest part to replicate, and it is free — as is a data channel beside existing media, which reuses the DTLS association you already paid for.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Do not use it for one-to-many broadcast. Per-viewer connection state and per-viewer bandwidth is exactly what a CDN exists to avoid. Low-latency HLS or DASH trades a few seconds for caching and effectively unbounded scale, and for an audience that does not talk back that trade is free.

Do not use it as a general client-server transport. If the peer on the other end is your own backend and the payload is messages, you are paying for signaling, STUN, TURN and ICE to get something a WebSocket does in one connection. Data channels are a bonus on an existing peer connection, not a reason to create one.

Do not assume peer-to-peer at scale. Mesh is quadratic in client uplink and dies around four or five participants on real networks. Anything beyond that needs a media server, and once the server is there most of the peer-to-peer arguments no longer apply.

Do not ship without the relay path tested. Some fraction of your users — driven entirely by their corporate firewalls and carrier NAT, not by your code — will only connect via TURN. If you have never forced iceTransportPolicy: "relay" in testing, that path is unverified in production.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "WebRTC is peer-to-peer."

✅ Reality: It is peer-to-peer capable, and most production deployments are not. Group calls need an SFU, server-side recording needs a server in the path, and voice agents need the media to reach a model. Peer-to-peer is the interesting default for exactly one case — 1:1 with no server-side consumer.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "WebRTC is a protocol."

✅ Reality: It is a bundle — ICE, STUN, TURN, DTLS, SRTP, SCTP and RTP, tied together by a browser API and an IETF applicability statement (RFC 8825). That is why debugging it means knowing which layer failed, and why "WebRTC is not working" is never a diagnosis.

❌ Misconception: "Encryption is a configuration option, like it is for HTTP."

✅ Reality: RFC 8827 requires SRTP for all media and forbids plaintext RTP; data channels must run over DTLS. There is no unencrypted mode to fall into, which also means you cannot read a WebRTC media stream with tcpdump alone — a real cost to debuggability that you accept up front.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Describing the happy path and stopping. "The two browsers exchange SDP and then media flows" leaves out the two places it actually breaks — signaling and ICE — which is what the follow-up will be about. Name the phases separately.

Quoting a relay-share percentage you cannot source. Figures in the 10–20% range circulate widely and vary enormously by user population. Say that it depends on the network mix, that you would measure it, and that it drives both the TURN bill and the latency floor — a stronger answer than a number you cannot defend.

Treating it as a video technology. Most current demand is audio and data — voice agents, transcription, control channels. Framing the topic around camera streams signals a conferencing tutorial.

Ignoring the server side, or forgetting that signaling is out of scope. Discussions escalate to topology within two questions, so if you cannot say when an SFU becomes mandatory and what it costs, the peer-to-peer answer reads as theoretical. And signaling being unspecified is the most distinctive fact about WebRTC and the most common omission.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Media encryption Mandatory — SRTP; plaintext RTP forbidden Data channels must use DTLS RFC 8827 §5.5
Opus frame sizes 2.5–60 ms (20 ms typical) Frame time is a direct latency term RFC 6716 §2
Opus bitrate range 6–510 kbit/s Speech is fine at 16–24 kbit/s RFC 6716 §2
Opus algorithmic delay 5–65.2 ms Configuration-dependent; part of the budget RFC 6716 §2
Default STUN port 3478 (TCP and UDP) TURN uses the same by default RFC 8489 §9
TURN allocation lifetime 600 s default Client must refresh or the relay drops RFC 8656 §3
Mesh connection count n(n-1)/2 per session Client uplink scales with n-1 Topology arithmetic
W3C spec status Recommendation, March 2025 The API is stable, not a moving target W3C WebRTC

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Sub-second is the whole point, but every server hop and the adaptive jitter buffer spend the budget — and the buffer grows silently on a lossy path
💰 Cost Peer-to-peer moves zero bytes through you; an SFU moves n(n-1) per room and TURN relays the full media stream. Relay share is the line item nobody forecasts
🔒 Security / visibility Encryption is mandatory and end-to-end to the SFU — which also means the SFU terminates it, so "end-to-end encrypted" needs qualifying once a media server exists
📈 Scale Per-participant connection state everywhere. Nothing is cacheable, nothing is stateless, and every participant is a resource on some server
🔧 Ops complexity The honest count is four services: signaling, STUN, TURN, SFU. A team that budgets for one is going to ship the other three under time pressure
🐛 Debuggability SRTP means you cannot read the media on the wire; getStats() and the SFU's own counters are your instrumentation, and they must be collected deliberately

16. Real World Usage

Voice agents are the current centre of gravity, and they changed the default answer. OpenAI's Realtime API documents WebRTC as the recommended transport for browser and mobile clients specifically for latency consistency, with WebSocket positioned for server-side connections. That split — WebRTC at the edge where networks are hostile, WebSocket in the data centre where they are not — is now the standard shape of a realtime AI stack.

Every group-calling product converged on the SFU independently. LiveKit, mediasoup and Janus all forward rather than mix, because forwarding keeps server CPU low and lets each receiver choose quality. mediasoup's design notes describe it as an unopinionated module rather than a standalone server — a good illustration of how much of a WebRTC product is still your own application code. And TURN is where the operational surprises live: Cloudflare's anycast writeup makes the point that a badly placed relay adds latency to exactly the users already struggling to connect.

17. Acronym Decoder

Topic name expansion — "Web Real-Time Communication" — teaches nothing about the mechanism, so it is skipped per the template rule. The acronyms that do carry mechanism (ICE, STUN, TURN, SFU, MCU, SDP) are decoded in their own notes.

📚 Reference Links

  • Capture — MDN: MediaDevices.getUserMedia()

  • The connection — MDN: RTCPeerConnection

  • The data path — MDN: RTCDataChannel

  • The normative definition — W3C: WebRTC — Real-Time Communication in Browsers

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What does getUserMedia require of the page? A secure context and explicit user permission.
Which state do you watch for "is the call up"? connectionState — not iceConnectionState, not signalingState.
Which two options make a data channel unreliable? maxRetransmits or maxPacketLifeTime (pick one, not both).

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Three objects cover the whole browser surface. getUserMedia returns a MediaStream of live tracks after a permission prompt, and only in a secure context. RTCPeerConnection is the engine — it gathers ICE candidates, negotiates via offers and answers, runs DTLS, keys SRTP, and carries tracks with congestion control built in. RTCDataChannel rides the same DTLS association for arbitrary bytes, with reliability you can turn down. The thing worth remembering is that RTCPeerConnection exposes three separate state machines, and picking the wrong one is the most common source of "the call says connected but there is no audio".

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

signalingState, iceConnectionState, connectionState — what does each actually tell you?

They report three different subsystems and they move independently. signalingState tracks the offer/answer machine — stable, have-local-offer, have-remote-offer and two pranswer states — so it tells you whether negotiation is in progress, and it returns to stable after every completed exchange including renegotiation. It says nothing about whether packets flow.

iceConnectionState tracks connectivity checks: new, checking, connected, completed, failed, disconnected, closed. connectionState is the aggregate you almost always want, because it folds in the DTLS transport as well — a connection can be ICE-connected while the DTLS handshake is still running or has failed, and only connectionState reflects that. The practical rule: drive user-visible call state from connectionState, use iceConnectionState when diagnosing which half broke, and treat disconnected as transient — it frequently recovers without an ICE restart, so tearing down on it produces dropped calls that would have survived.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

When do you reach for a data channel instead of the WebSocket you already have?

🎯 Really testing: whether you weigh an existing connection against a new dependency, rather than reaching for the newer API.

The data channel wins when the peer connection already exists and the traffic is latency-sensitive and peer-directed — cursor positions, game state, control messages between two clients. It reuses the DTLS association, so there is no extra handshake and no extra server hop, and it lets you turn reliability off: setting maxRetransmits: 0 with ordered: false gives you UDP-like delivery, which is correct for state that is superseded by the next update and pointless to retransmit.

The WebSocket wins for anything that is really client-to-server, anything the server must see, and anything that has to work before the peer connection is up — including the signaling that establishes it. Standing up ICE, STUN, TURN and signaling purely to get a data channel is inverted engineering. The honest framing is that a data channel is a free side effect of a media session you already needed; it is almost never a reason to create one.

4. Quick Comparison Table

API Gives you Fails when When you'd actually pick it
getUserMedia Live audio/video tracks Insecure context, permission denied, device in use Any capture from a browser
RTCPeerConnection ICE, DTLS, SRTP, RTP, congestion control No valid candidate pair, DTLS failure Every WebRTC session — this is the engine
RTCDataChannel Ordered or unordered bytes over SCTP/DTLS Only after the peer connection is up Low-latency peer-directed data beside existing media
(WebSocket, for contrast) Client↔server messages Proxy idle timeouts Signaling, and anything the server must see

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The ordering constraint the diagram encodes is that tracks must be added before the offer is created, because the offer describes them. Adding a track later is legal and triggers negotiationneeded, which means a whole new offer/answer exchange — so "add video mid-call" is a renegotiation, not a method call. The data channel branches off the same DTLS association rather than establishing its own, which is why creating one on an existing connection is nearly free and why it also triggers renegotiation the first time.

The reliability knobs on a data channel are mutually exclusive: maxRetransmits caps retry count, maxPacketLifeTime caps time spent trying, and setting both is an error. ordered is independent and defaults to true. The four useful combinations run from fully reliable and ordered (a file transfer) through unordered with zero retransmits (live cursor position, where the next update makes the lost one irrelevant).

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Do not drive call state from iceConnectionState. It reports connectivity only, so it can read connected while DTLS is still handshaking or has already failed. Use connectionState for anything the user sees, and reserve the ICE state for diagnosis.

Do not tear down on disconnected. It is a transient signal — a brief loss of connectivity checks — and it recovers on its own frequently enough that reacting immediately converts recoverable blips into dropped calls. Wait, then restart ICE if it persists.

Do not call getUserMedia at page load. The permission prompt is unbounded wall-clock time and a hostile first impression; request it when the user commits to joining, and pre-warm the peer connection instead if you want to save latency.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "addTrack after the connection is up just starts sending."

✅ Reality: It fires negotiationneeded and requires a fresh offer/answer round trip through signaling. Any feature that adds media mid-call — screen share, turning the camera on — is a renegotiation, which is exactly why glare handling matters in a symmetric app.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "The data channel is a separate connection, so it has its own setup cost."

✅ Reality: It is SCTP encapsulated in the DTLS association the media already uses, sharing the same ICE-negotiated path. Once a peer connection exists, a data channel costs one renegotiation and no new handshake — which is what makes it attractive beside media and unattractive on its own.

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What does WebRTC specify about signaling? Nothing beyond the need to exchange session descriptions.
What travels over it? SDP offer, SDP answer, and a stream of ICE candidates.
What is glare? Both peers offer at once; resolved by polite/impolite roles with rollback.
Can the signaling server go away mid-call? Yes — once media flows, it is out of the path until renegotiation.
Why trickle rather than wait? Checks start on early candidates while TURN allocation is still in flight.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Signaling is the channel that carries the SDP offer, the SDP answer and the ICE candidates between two peers before they can talk directly — and WebRTC deliberately does not specify it. JSEP says only that session descriptions must be exchanged; addressing, retransmission, forking and glare are left to the application, which in practice means a WebSocket service you write. It matters because it is the first thing you build and the first thing that breaks: it holds identity, room membership and authorization, and once media is flowing it drops out of the path entirely.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why did the spec leave signaling out, and what does that cost you?

The stated reason in JSEP is decoupling: the media plane should not care how offers and answers reach the far side, so addressing, retransmission, forking and glare handling are explicitly the application's problem. That was the right call in 1990s-telephony terms — SIP, XMPP and half a dozen proprietary systems already existed, and mandating one would have made WebRTC unusable inside all the others. The messages themselves are just text, so any transport that can move a string bidirectionally will do.

What it costs you is that every WebRTC project starts by building a stateful, authenticated, low-latency message router before any media exists. That service ends up owning things the media plane has no concept of: who is allowed in a room, which peer is the caller, what happens when someone reloads the page mid-negotiation, and how a second offer is reconciled with one already in flight. None of those problems are hard individually, and all of them are yours.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Which transport would you build signaling on, and what breaks with each?

🎯 Really testing: whether you recognise this as an ordinary messaging design problem rather than something WebRTC-specific.

WebSocket is the default and usually correct: it is bidirectional, low-latency, and the server needs to push an incoming call to a client that did not ask for it. The cost is the usual WebSocket operational tax — sticky sessions or a shared pub/sub layer so that two peers connected to different signaling instances can reach each other, plus proxy idle timeouts, heartbeats and reconnect-with-resume logic. Server-Sent Events plus ordinary POSTs is a defensible alternative when server push is the only asymmetry you need, and it inherits HTTP auth and observability for free.

The variant worth knowing is that signaling need not be a long-lived connection at all. OpenAI's Realtime API establishes a WebRTC session by having the browser POST its SDP offer over HTTPS and receive the answer in the response — one request/response, no signaling server, because there is exactly one known peer and no room membership to manage. That is the right shape whenever the far end is a fixed service rather than another user, and it is a good example of the general rule: the signaling design follows from how peers discover each other, not from WebRTC.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What runs out or breaks first as signaling scales, and how does it present?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard second incident of any WebRTC product — the first is TURN.

Connection state runs out first, on the signaling tier rather than the media tier. Every idle client holds an open WebSocket waiting for an incoming call, so the service carries far more connections than active calls — file descriptors, per-connection memory and per-instance limits bite well before CPU. The second scarce resource is routing: if peers on different instances must reach each other, every message crosses a pub/sub hop whose fan-out grows with instance count rather than call volume.

It presents as calls that fail to start while calls in progress stay perfectly healthy — the diagnostic signature worth memorising, because it points at signaling rather than media. A rolling deploy does the same thing deliberately: draining an instance disconnects every idle client at once, they reconnect within seconds, and the herd looks like an attack. Existing calls survive it because media does not traverse signaling, and that asymmetry is what tells you where to look.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the signaling layer for a product with rooms, reconnects, and a voice agent that can be invited into a call.

🎯 Really testing: whether you treat signaling as a stateful distributed system with its own SLOs, or as a message relay you can bolt on.

The highest-stakes constraint is that signaling holds authoritative room state while being the tier most likely to be restarted. So keep connection handling stateless and put room membership in a shared store, with the WebSocket instances as interchangeable front ends subscribed to per-room channels. A client can then reconnect to any instance and resynchronise, and a deploy costs a reconnect storm rather than data loss. Route peer messages through the same pub/sub rather than instance affinity, because affinity turns every deploy into a correctness problem.

The message set stays deliberately small: join, leave, offer, answer, candidate, and a room-state snapshot on connect. Authorization happens once at connect against a short-lived token; membership is checked on every join rather than cached client-side. Inviting the agent is then just another participant joining — the worker connects like a client, receives room state, and negotiates with the SFU. Resisting a special path for the agent is what keeps one system instead of two.

The failure I would monitor first is time-to-connected split by phase — signaling round trip, ICE gathering, DTLS — because aggregate join latency hides which of the three regressed and they have unrelated fixes. Second is reconnect rate, whose rising baseline is the early signal of a proxy or load-balancer timeout that will eventually present as "calls randomly fail to start".

4. Quick Comparison Table

Transport Push? Auth story What breaks When you'd actually pick it
WebSocket Native Token at connect Idle timeouts, sticky routing, reconnect storms The default — mutual push between unknown peers
SSE + POST Server→client only Ordinary HTTP auth Connection per client, no client push When only the server needs to initiate
HTTPS request/response None Ordinary HTTP auth Cannot deliver an incoming call One known peer, no room state — the Realtime-API shape
SIP Native Established telco model Complexity, and nobody on your team knows it Interop with existing telephony, never greenfield
Long polling Emulated Ordinary HTTP auth Latency, connection churn Only where WebSocket is genuinely blocked

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Three message types, and only three. The offer describes what the caller can send and receive; the answer is the callee's intersection of that with its own capabilities; the candidates are transport addresses discovered asynchronously. Everything else in a real signaling protocol — presence, room lists, mute state, chat — is your application, not WebRTC, and it is worth keeping that boundary visible in the code because the three protocol messages have ordering rules the rest do not.

The ordering rule that causes most bugs is that candidates can arrive before the description they belong to. addIceCandidate fails if there is no remote description yet, so any real implementation buffers early candidates and flushes them after setRemoteDescription. Trickle ICE makes this the normal case rather than a race: candidates are emitted as they are discovered, deliberately in parallel with gathering, precisely so connectivity checks can begin before the slow relayed candidate appears.

Glare is the other structural problem, and it has a standard solution. If both peers hit negotiationneeded at once, both send offers and both reject the other's. The perfect-negotiation pattern assigns one peer the polite role: on collision the polite peer rolls back its own local description and accepts the incoming offer, while the impolite peer ignores the collision and wins. The payoff is that both sides run identical code with no caller/callee branching — which matters more than it sounds, because the alternative is two code paths that diverge over time.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable is call setup success rate, and signaling owns most of it. Media failures degrade quality; signaling failures mean the call never starts, which users report as "the app is broken" rather than "the audio was poor". Because signaling is a normal stateful service, its failure modes are the normal ones — deploys, connection limits, proxy timeouts — and they are far more common than anything in the media stack.

The second observable is join latency. Two signaling round trips sit on the critical path before any media can flow, so a signaling service placed far from the user adds directly to time-to-first-audio. That is a concrete argument for regional signaling endpoints in a voice-agent product, where the whole budget is a few hundred milliseconds.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

// The two rules that cause most signaling bugs: buffer early candidates, and be polite.
const polite = !isCaller;            // one side must yield on collision
let makingOffer = false, ignoreOffer = false;
const pending = [];                  // candidates that arrived before the description

pc.onnegotiationneeded = async () => {
  makingOffer = true;
  await pc.setLocalDescription();     // implicit createOffer since 2020
  ws.send(JSON.stringify({ description: pc.localDescription }));
  makingOffer = false;
};

ws.onmessage = async ({ data }) => {
  const { description, candidate } = JSON.parse(data);
  if (description) {
    const collision = description.type === "offer" &&
                      (makingOffer || pc.signalingState !== "stable");
    ignoreOffer = !polite && collision;          // impolite peer wins the race
    if (ignoreOffer) return;
    await pc.setRemoteDescription(description);  // rollback happens implicitly if polite
    while (pending.length) await pc.addIceCandidate(pending.shift());
    if (description.type === "offer") {
      await pc.setLocalDescription();
      ws.send(JSON.stringify({ description: pc.localDescription }));
    }
  } else if (candidate) {
    if (pc.remoteDescription) await pc.addIceCandidate(candidate);
    else pending.push(candidate);                // the buffer that fixes the ordering race
  }
};

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

The handler above, during a renegotiation where both sides add a track simultaneously — the glare case.

📥 [0] Both peers fire negotiationneeded at t≈0             signalingState: stable
    │
    ▼
📡 [1] A sends offer (makingOffer=true)                     A: have-local-offer
      B sends offer (makingOffer=true)                      B: have-local-offer
    │
    ▼
⚠️ [2] Each receives the other's offer while non-stable → collision detected
      A is impolite → ignoreOffer=true, drops B's offer      A: have-local-offer
      B is polite   → implicit rollback, accepts A's offer   B: have-remote-offer
    │
    ▼
🔗 [3] B answers A's offer                                   B: stable
      A applies the answer                                   A: stable
    │
    ▼
🔍 [4] Candidates that arrived during [1]–[3] flush from `pending`
    │
    ▼
🎯 [5] One negotiation completed, B's original intent re-fires
       via a second negotiationneeded — no deadlock, no lost track

  1. Both sides in have-local-offer at once is the definition of glare, and it is not rare — any event that triggers renegotiation on both peers (adding a track, a codec change, an ICE restart) produces it.

  2. The collision test is makingOffer || signalingState !== "stable", not the state alone. Checking state by itself races against the async setLocalDescription, which is why the flag exists.

  3. Only one peer yields, and the roles must be deterministic. Caller versus callee, or comparing peer IDs — anything stable works, but both sides must agree, and getting that agreement from signaling is the point.

  4. The dropped intent is not lost. The polite peer's rollback is implicit in modern browsers, and its own reason for negotiating re-fires negotiationneeded once the connection is stable again. Implementations that treat the collision as an error and tear down convert a resolvable race into a failed call.

10. When TO Use This

Whenever two peers who do not already know each other's transport addresses need a WebRTC session — which is every case except a fixed, known service endpoint.

When room membership, presence or authorization is part of the product. These have to live somewhere, and signaling is where they naturally belong because it is already the authenticated, stateful tier.

When you need renegotiation mid-call — adding screen share, switching codecs, an ICE restart after a network change. All of these are new offer/answer exchanges, so signaling must stay reachable for the life of the call even though it carries no media.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Do not build a signaling service when there is exactly one known peer. If the far end is a fixed API endpoint, a single HTTPS POST carrying the offer and returning the answer is the whole design — no connection state, no rooms, no reconnect logic. Building a WebSocket tier for this is inventing a distributed system you did not need.

Do not put media or bulk data through it. Signaling is a low-volume control channel; the moment file transfer or telemetry starts flowing through the same WebSocket, its connection limits and latency profile change and it stops being the thing you sized.

Do not rely on it staying connected for the call to survive. Media flows peer-to-peer or via the SFU once established, so a signaling outage should degrade to "no new calls, no renegotiation" rather than dropping existing ones. If your client tears down the peer connection when the WebSocket closes, you have coupled two failure domains for no reason.

Do not use instance affinity to route between peers. Sticky sessions make it work in staging and make every deploy a correctness question. A shared pub/sub layer is the boring, correct answer.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Signaling is part of WebRTC, I just haven't found the API yet."

✅ Reality: JSEP explicitly declines to specify it — the implementation is "totally decoupled from the actual mechanism by which these offers and answers are communicated", including addressing, retransmission, forking and glare. There is no API because there is no spec.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Signaling ends once the call connects."

✅ Reality: It goes idle, which is not the same thing. Every renegotiation — screen share, track added, ICE restart after a Wi-Fi to cellular switch — is a fresh offer/answer through signaling. A client that closes the WebSocket after connecting cannot recover from a network change.

❌ Misconception: "Glare is an edge case you can handle later."

✅ Reality: It fires on ordinary renegotiation whenever both sides act at once, which happens routinely in symmetric applications. The perfect-negotiation pattern exists because the alternative — separate caller and callee code paths — is where the bugs accumulate.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Saying "signaling is out of scope" and stopping. Correct fact, incomplete answer. The follow-up is always what you would build, so continue into the transport choice, the three message types, and where room state lives.

Describing signaling as a stateless relay. It holds authorization, room membership and the caller/callee roles glare resolution depends on. Presenting it as a dumb pipe means you have not designed one.

Ignoring the ordering problem between candidates and descriptions. Every real implementation buffers early candidates; not mentioning it suggests experience from a tutorial where both peers ran in the same tab.

Forgetting that renegotiation exists. Answering only for call setup misses screen sharing, ICE restart and network migration, which is where the interesting failures are — and treating the resulting reconnect storm as a client bug rather than a deploy-strategy question.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Signaling round trips before media 2 (offer, answer) Plus trickling candidates in parallel RFC 3264 · RFC 8838
What JSEP specifies about transport Nothing "Left entirely up to the application" RFC 8829 §3
signalingState values 6 stable, have-local-offer, have-remote-offer, two pranswer states, closed W3C WebRTC / MDN
Candidate exchange model Incremental Trickle sends candidates during gathering, not after RFC 8838 §1

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Two signaling round trips sit on the critical path to first audio — a distant signaling region costs you directly, before any media exists
💰 Cost Cheap in bandwidth, expensive in idle connections: you pay for every logged-in client waiting for a call that may not come
🔒 Security / visibility The natural place for authentication and room authorization — and therefore the natural place to get it wrong, since the media plane will not re-check
📈 Scale Bounded by concurrent connections and pub/sub fan-out, not by call volume. These diverge, and only one of them is on your product dashboard
🔧 Ops complexity An ordinary stateful WebSocket service with all the usual taxes — sticky routing or shared state, heartbeats, draining, reconnect storms
🐛 Debuggability The one plaintext part of a WebRTC session. Log the SDP and the candidate stream; it is the only place you can see what the peers agreed

16. Real World Usage

The single-request variant is now common in AI products. OpenAI's Realtime API has the browser POST its SDP offer to a developer-controlled server, which forwards it with session configuration and returns the answer, using a short-lived ephemeral key so the browser never holds a real API key. There is no signaling server because there is one peer and no room state — a clean demonstration that "signaling" is a problem shape rather than a component. Conferencing platforms went the other way entirely: in an SFU system the signaling service owns rooms, participant lists, permissions and track subscriptions, and the media server is comparatively simple.

The classic outage is a proxy idle timeout nobody set. A signaling WebSocket carries nothing between calls, so an intermediary with a 60-second idle timeout closes it silently: clients appear online, incoming calls are never delivered, and existing calls are unaffected because media does not traverse signaling. Application-level heartbeats are the fix, and the asymmetric symptom is the diagnosis.

17. Acronym Decoder

JSEP — JavaScript Session Establishment Protocol.

  • Session Establishment — it defines the state machine for creating and applying offers and answers, not the wire protocol that carries them. That distinction is the entire topic of this note.

  • JavaScript — the model was written around the browser API surface, which is why its vocabulary (setLocalDescription, rollback, negotiationneeded) matches the W3C spec so closely.

Decoding it is worth the line because the name is what tells you where the boundary sits: JSEP owns establishment, your application owns transport.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • ICE, STUN & TURN (81-ice-stun-turn.md) — where the candidates come from and why trickling matters.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • A single HTTPS request/response — correct whenever there is one known peer; no connection state at all.

  • SIP — the incumbent in telephony interop, and the reason WebRTC declined to mandate a signaling protocol in the first place.

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • Sticky sessions / session affinity (Section 11) — what you use if you do not have shared room state, and what you should avoid if you can.

  • API authentication (Section 10) — short-lived tokens at connect time, which is where the ephemeral-key pattern comes from.

  • Topologies — mesh vs SFU vs MCU (85-topologies-mesh-sfu-mcu.md) — signaling holds the room state the topology operates on.

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

The framing is usually "design a video calling product" or "add a voice agent to an existing app", and signaling is the component candidates skip. A strong answer names it as a stateful service with its own scaling story, separates connection handling from room state, explains how two peers on different instances reach each other, and says what happens to in-progress calls during a deploy. A weak answer draws a box labelled "signaling server" and moves on to codecs.

Topology diagram

The dotted lines carry the point: media never traverses the signaling tier, so signaling can be restarted, scaled or deployed without touching calls in progress. The two peers deliberately land on different instances to show that affinity is not required once room state is shared.

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
10x idle clients Concurrent WebSocket connections per instance — file descriptors and per-connection memory, long before CPU Horizontal scale on connection count rather than call count; raise ulimit; measure idle connections separately from active calls
100x Pub/sub fan-out — every instance subscribed to every active room's channel Shard rooms across channels; route by room hash so an instance subscribes only to rooms it holds members for
1000x Global user base: signaling round trips cross continents and dominate join latency Regional signaling endpoints with room state replicated or pinned per region; accept that cross-region rooms pay the extra RTT

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • Reconnect storm during deploys at 10x. Draining an instance disconnects every idle client at once; the burst looks like an attack and can push remaining instances past their connection limits.

  • Pub/sub becomes the bottleneck at 100x. Message rate grows with instances × active rooms rather than with calls, so the supposedly cheap tier becomes the expensive one.

  • The 3am version: a proxy idle timeout. Clients believe they are online, incoming calls are never delivered, existing calls are fine, and every dashboard is green because the failure is the absence of a message.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • Call setup success rate, split by phase — signaling round trip, ICE gathering, DTLS. The aggregate hides which one regressed, and the three have unrelated fixes.

  • Idle versus active connection count — they scale independently, and only the second appears on a product dashboard. Alarm on connections per instance against the configured limit.

  • Reconnect rate baseline — a slow rise is the early warning for a proxy or load-balancer timeout, weeks before it presents as calls failing to start.

  • How WebRTC applies it — RFC 8829: JavaScript Session Establishment Protocol (JSEP)

  • What ends up in the media section — RFC 8834: Media Transport and Use of RTP in WebRTC

  • Bonus — WebRTC for the Curious: Signaling

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What is an answer, precisely? The intersection of the offer's capabilities with the answerer's own.
Which line carries the DTLS identity? a=fingerprint — the certificate hash bound by signaling.
What do a=sendrecv / sendonly / recvonly / inactive set? Direction, per media section, independently each way.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

SDP is the text blob two peers exchange to agree on a session. The offer lists everything the caller can do — media sections for each track, codecs with their payload types, ICE username and password, the DTLS fingerprint and the setup role. The answer returns the same structure narrowed to what the callee also supports, and that intersection is the session. It is old, line-oriented and awkward to read, but the fields that matter are few: m= sections, a=rtpmap for codecs, a=fingerprint for identity, and the direction attribute.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

What is actually in an offer, and which parts decide the session?

Structurally an offer has a session-level block and then one media section per track or transceiver, each beginning with an m= line naming the media type and the payload types it will accept. Under each section, a=rtpmap maps payload numbers to codec names — this is where Opus, VP8 or H.264 appear — and a=fmtp carries codec parameters. a=ice-ufrag and a=ice-pwd are the credentials that authenticate ICE connectivity checks, so they tie the candidate exchange to this specific session.

Three attributes do most of the deciding. a=fingerprint carries a hash of the DTLS certificate, which is what makes signaling security-critical: an attacker who can rewrite that line can insert themselves into the media path, because DTLS will happily authenticate whatever certificate the fingerprint names. a=setup decides which side acts as DTLS client (active) versus server (passive), with actpass in the offer meaning "you choose". And the direction attribute is per media section and asymmetric, so a section can be sendonly from one peer and recvonly at the other — which is how a receive-only viewer or a send-only agent is expressed.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

How much should an application actually touch the SDP?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know that SDP munging is a real, fragile practice — and when it is nonetheless the only option.

The default should be not at all. The browser generates SDP from the transceivers and codec preferences you configured, and supported APIs cover most of what people reach into the text for: setCodecPreferences to order codecs, RTCRtpSender.setParameters for bitrate and encodings, transceiver direction for send/receive control. Those survive browser updates.

Editing the string directly — "SDP munging" — persists because a few things still have no API: forcing a bitrate line, stripping a codec a gateway mishandles, interoperating with SIP equipment that rejects what the browser emits. It works, and it is brittle in a specific way: the grammar is ordered, payload numbers are session-scoped, and an edit correct in one browser version quietly desynchronises m= sections in the next — producing a call that negotiates and then carries no media. Treat munging as an interop workaround with an owner and a test, never as configuration.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Attribute Carries Why it matters Failure if wrong
m= Media type, port, payload types One per track/transceiver; order is significant Sections desynchronise, media stops
a=rtpmap / a=fmtp Codec name and parameters Where Opus / VP8 / H.264 are negotiated No common codec — negotiation succeeds, no media
a=ice-ufrag / a=ice-pwd ICE credentials Authenticates connectivity checks for this session Checks rejected, connection stuck in checking
a=fingerprint DTLS certificate hash The entire identity binding for the media plane An attacker who rewrites it can MITM the media
a=setup DTLS client/server role actpass in offer, concrete in answer Both sides passive — handshake never starts
a=sendrecv etc. Direction, per section Expresses one-way media cleanly Unexpected silence in one direction

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The asymmetry is the mechanism. An offer is a superset — a declaration of capability — and the answer is the binding decision, so the session is always defined by the answer rather than by any negotiation between equals. Anything absent from the answer is not in the session, which is why "we both support H.264 but there is no video" almost always resolves to a media section the answerer narrowed or rejected.

Direction is per section and per peer, which is more expressive than people expect. A voice agent that only listens can answer recvonly on the audio section while its own synthesised track occupies a separate sendonly section. A rejected section is signalled by setting its port to zero rather than by removing it, because the ordering of m= sections must be preserved across the exchange — removing one would shift every later section's meaning.

Renegotiation reuses the same machinery. Screen share, a codec-preference change and an ICE restart all produce a fresh offer with new a=ice-ufrag and a=ice-pwd, and signalingState leaves stable and returns. There is no separate "modify" operation, which means one code path handles setup and every subsequent change.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Do not hand-parse SDP to extract state. Codec support, selected candidate pair, bitrate and direction are all available through getStats() and the transceiver APIs, which are stable. Regexes over SDP break on the next browser release, and they break silently.

Do not treat the signaling channel as untrusted-but-fine. The DTLS fingerprint travels in the SDP, so signaling integrity is media-plane security. An attacker who can modify signaling messages can substitute their own fingerprint and terminate the media. Authenticate and encrypt signaling accordingly.

Do not munge SDP as a routine configuration mechanism. Prefer setCodecPreferences and setParameters; reserve string editing for interop workarounds that have an owner, a comment explaining the gateway it exists for, and a test that fails when it stops being necessary.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "The offer and answer negotiate — both sides give a bit."

✅ Reality: The offer proposes everything the offerer supports and the answer unilaterally selects. There is no round of counter-proposals; the answer is the session, and anything it omits is gone until someone offers again.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "SDP is just a description, so tampering with it in transit is a privacy issue at most."

✅ Reality: It carries a=fingerprint, which is the sole binding between the signaling identity and the DTLS certificate that encrypts the media. Rewriting that line is a complete media-plane compromise — which is why WebRTC's security architecture assumes the signaling channel is authenticated.

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The four ICE candidate types? Host, server-reflexive, peer-reflexive, relayed.
Type preferences, highest to lowest? 126 host, 110 peer-reflexive, 100 server-reflexive, 0 relayed.
What does STUN actually return? The source address the server saw — your NAT's mapping.
Default STUN/TURN port? 3478, TCP and UDP.
Default TURN allocation lifetime? 600 seconds; the client must refresh it.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

ICE is the algorithm that finds a working path between two endpoints behind NAT. Each side gathers candidate addresses — its local address, the address a STUN server saw it from, and a relayed address on a TURN server — exchanges them through signaling, then probes every pair with STUN checks and nominates the highest-priority pair that works. STUN is a one-message question, "what source address do you see?", and costs nothing. TURN is a full media relay, so it costs bandwidth and adds a hop, and it is what you fall back to when both sides are behind NATs that will not cooperate.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Walk me through what ICE actually does, from gathering to a nominated pair.

Gathering produces up to three candidate kinds per interface. The host candidate is the socket's local address. The server-reflexive candidate comes from a STUN Binding request to a public server, which replies with the source address it observed — the mapping your NAT created, and the address a peer would have to aim at. The relayed candidate comes from a TURN Allocate, reserving an address on the TURN server that forwards to you. Each is discovered independently, and trickle ICE emits them as they appear.

Both sides then pair every local candidate with every remote one, sort by a priority formula, and send STUN Binding requests along each pair in order. A pair is valid only when checks succeed in both directions, because NAT filtering is directional — A's outbound packet creates the mapping that admits B's. Peer-reflexive candidates are discovered here: a check arriving from an address nobody advertised becomes a new candidate. The controlling agent nominates a valid pair with a flagged STUN request, and media starts.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

STUN is nearly free and TURN is not. How do you decide what to deploy, and what do you actually pay for?

🎯 Really testing: whether you understand TURN as a bandwidth-bearing service rather than a signalling helper — most people size it like a STUN server.

STUN is stateless, one request/response, a few dozen bytes; you can run it on almost nothing. TURN carries every media packet in both directions for the whole call, so its bandwidth is session count times bitrate, and it holds per-allocation state on a 600-second default lifetime clients must refresh. That is the whole deployment decision: STUN is a utility, TURN is infrastructure with a capacity plan and a bill.

You cannot skip TURN, though. Some fraction of users sit behind NATs or firewalls where no direct path exists, and for them relay is the difference between a working product and failed calls. What you control is the fraction and its cost: place relays close to users so the extra leg is short, use TCP/TLS on 443 only as a last resort because it reintroduces head-of-line blocking on media, and instrument relay share as a first-class metric. The number varies enormously by user population — corporate desktop and consumer mobile are not comparable — so the honest answer is that you measure it rather than quote it.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What runs out first on a TURN deployment, and how does the failure present?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard capacity surprise once a WebRTC product lands its first large enterprise customer.

Bandwidth runs out first. Every relayed session pushes full media through the server in both directions, so a video product hits network-interface limits long before CPU. Allocation state is the second ceiling — each allocation holds a relayed address plus permissions and timers, and each refresh is a request to process. Egress cost is the third, and in a cloud deployment it is frequently the product's largest line item.

It presents as a quality problem rather than a connectivity one, which is why it gets misdiagnosed. A saturated relay drops or delays packets for everyone traversing it; bandwidth estimation on each client responds by lowering bitrate, so users report degraded audio while every connectivity metric stays green. The identifying symptom is that degradation correlates with relayed sessions specifically — visible only if relay share and per-path quality are separate metrics.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Where do you place STUN and TURN for a global product, and how does that interact with your media servers?

🎯 Really testing: whether you treat the relay as part of the latency path rather than as a fallback that only affects reliability.

The driving constraint is that a relayed path is a detour — client → TURN → peer or SFU — so a relay in the wrong region can add more latency than the media server itself. Relays belong at the edge, near users, not co-located with a central media tier. Anycast gets that without client-side selection logic, and Cloudflare's writeup of TURN over anycast is a good treatment of why placement is a latency decision. STUN placement barely matters by comparison: one round trip during gathering, nothing afterwards.

In an SFU architecture TURN's job shrinks dramatically. The client is not reaching an arbitrary peer behind an unknown NAT; it is reaching a server with a public address, which succeeds directly in the large majority of cases. Relay is then needed mainly for clients whose egress blocks UDP entirely, and for those the useful configuration is TURN over TLS on 443, which looks like ordinary HTTPS to a restrictive firewall. That is a deliberate quality trade — TCP under media means head-of-line blocking — and the right one, because a degraded call beats no call.

The failure I would monitor first is relay share by network and region, because it moves for reasons outside your control: one enterprise customer changing firewall policy can shift a slice of sessions onto relay overnight, and the first symptom is a bandwidth graph rather than an alert. Second is the time-to-connected distribution, whose rising tail means checks are failing on preferred pairs and falling through to relay.

4. Quick Comparison Table

STUN TURN When you'd actually pick it
What it does Reports the source address it saw Relays all media through itself STUN discovers; TURN carries
Traffic through it One request/response The entire call, both directions TURN cost scales with minutes × bitrate
State held None Allocation, permissions, timers (600 s default) TURN needs a capacity plan; STUN does not
Latency added One RTT during gathering An extra leg for the whole call Relay placement is a latency decision
Candidate priority Server-reflexive, preference 100 Relayed, preference 0 ICE uses relay only when nothing better works
Deploy where Anywhere public At the edge, near users Central relays punish exactly the users already struggling

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The priority formula is the mechanism, not trivia. RFC 8445 computes candidate priority as (2^24 × type preference) + (2^8 × local preference) + (256 − component ID), with recommended type preferences of 126 for host, 110 for peer-reflexive, 100 for server-reflexive and 0 for relayed. Because the type term is multiplied by 2^24, it dominates absolutely: a relayed candidate can never outrank a reflexive one regardless of the other terms. That is why a working direct path is always chosen over a working relay, and why forcing relay in testing requires an explicit policy rather than hoping.

Pair priority combines both sides asymmetrically — 2^32 × MIN(G,D) + 2 × MAX(G,D) + (G>D ? 1 : 0) for controlling and controlled agents G and D. The shape matters more than the formula: both peers derive the same ordering from the same inputs, so they check pairs in the same sequence with no extra coordination.

Whether a direct path exists comes down to NAT behaviour on two independent axes. Mapping decides whether the NAT reuses one external port for all destinations or allocates one per destination; filtering decides who may send back through it. Endpoint-independent mapping is what makes STUN useful at all — the address the STUN server saw is usable by your peer only if the NAT reuses it. When both sides allocate per destination, neither can predict the other's port, and relay is the only option. That is the mechanical reason TURN exists. (→ 82-nat-types-why-p2p-fails.md)

|0 0|     STUN Message Type     |         Message Length          |

|                         Magic Cookie                            |

📚 Adapted from RFC 8489 §5 and §14.2. XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS is XORed with the magic cookie specifically so that NATs performing naive payload rewriting do not corrupt it — a detail worth knowing because it is the one field the whole protocol exists to deliver.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable is connection success rate, and ICE owns the part of it that your code cannot influence. A call that never reaches connected is almost always an ICE outcome — no valid pair, or a valid pair only via a relay you did not deploy. Because the determining factor is the user's NAT and firewall rather than anything you ship, this is the one part of the stack where the failure population is defined externally and can change without a deploy on your side.

The second observable is the TURN bandwidth bill, which is relay share multiplied by session minutes multiplied by bitrate. It is unusual among infrastructure costs in being driven by your users' network conditions, so it is both hard to forecast and capable of stepping up overnight when one large customer changes a firewall rule.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# Does my NAT allow a direct path at all? Ask a STUN server what it sees.
# Repeat against two different STUN servers: same reported port = endpoint-independent
# mapping (direct path likely). Different ports = symmetric NAT, relay required.
turnutils_stunclient -p 3478 stun.example.net

# Verify the relay path works before a customer verifies it for you.
turnutils_uclient -v -u demo -w secret -p 3478 turn.example.net

// Force every candidate through TURN. This is how you test the fallback deliberately.
const pc = new RTCPeerConnection({
  iceServers: [
    { urls: "stun:stun.example.net:3478" },
    { urls: ["turn:turn.example.net:3478?transport=udp",
             "turns:turn.example.net:443?transport=tcp"],   // TLS/443 for hostile egress
      username: shortLivedUser, credential: shortLivedSecret },
  ],
  iceTransportPolicy: "relay",     // "all" in production; "relay" in the test that matters
});
// Which pair actually won, and was it relayed?
const stats = await pc.getStats();
// look for candidate-pair with state "succeeded" and nominated true, then its localCandidateId

TURN credentials must be short-lived and derived per session — a static username and password in client JavaScript is a bandwidth-theft invitation, since anyone can relay arbitrary traffic through it.

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

The configuration above, one call between a home user behind an ordinary router and an office user behind a symmetric NAT.

    │
    ▼
🔍 [1] A: host 192.168.1.24:51820                                  t ≈ 1 ms
        A: srflx 203.0.113.9:51820  (STUN, 1 RTT)                  t ≈ 30 ms
        A: relay 198.51.100.4:49200 (TURN Allocate, lifetime 600s) t ≈ 65 ms
    │
    ▼
🔍 [2] B: host 10.20.4.7:52310
        B: srflx 198.51.100.77:41002  ← port differs per destination (symmetric)
        B: relay 198.51.100.4:49318
    │
    ▼
🔗 [3] Pair checks in priority order:
        host↔host      (126) → no response, different networks
        srflx↔srflx    (100) → A's packets reach a port B's NAT will not accept;
                               B's packets come from a port A never advertised
        (A learns B's peer-reflexive candidate here, but B's mapping is
         per-destination, so it is not reusable)
    │
    ▼
🔁 [4] relay↔srflx (0) → succeeds. Nominated.                      t ≈ 210 ms
    │
    ▼
🎯 [5] DTLS over the relayed pair, SRTP flows                      first audio ≈ 280 ms
        every packet now traverses 198.51.100.4 in both directions

  1. The host candidate is free and the relayed candidate is slowest. That ordering is why trickle ICE exists: checks on host and reflexive candidates begin while the TURN Allocate is still in flight, so the relay costs setup time only when it is actually needed.

  2. B's symmetric NAT is the whole story. Its mapping is address-and-port-dependent, so the port it showed the STUN server is not the port it uses toward A. A's checks arrive somewhere no longer valid, and neither peer can do anything about it.

  3. Peer-reflexive discovery happens but does not save this call. A learns a new candidate from B's incoming check — exactly what peer-reflexive candidates are for — but a per-destination mapping is not reusable for a different pairing.

  4. Relay wins only because everything better failed. Preference 0 means the relayed pair is nominated only when no higher-priority pair is valid, which is the mechanism guaranteeing you never pay for a relay you did not need. The cost is then fixed for the session: every packet traverses the relay in both directions until the call ends.

10. When TO Use This

Always, in any WebRTC deployment. ICE is how the connection is established, including the trivial same-network case. The decision is not whether to use it but which candidate types you make available.

STUN whenever peers may be behind NAT — effectively always. One round trip during gathering converts a large fraction of otherwise-impossible connections into direct paths.

TURN whenever you have real users rather than a demo, and TURN over TLS on 443 as an explicit second tier when you have enterprise users. The first is the difference between a working product and failed calls; the second defeats restrictive egress at the cost of TCP under the media, which is the right trade when the alternative is failure.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Do not deploy relays centrally to save money. A relay is an extra leg, so a single region punishes exactly the users who already could not connect directly. Edge placement is the design; a central relay is a latency tax on your worst-served users.

Do not ship static TURN credentials. Anything in client code can be extracted and used to relay arbitrary traffic on your bill. Credentials should be short-lived and issued per session by your backend.

Do not size TURN like a STUN server. It carries full media bidirectionally with per-allocation state, and the resulting saturation looks like a quality problem rather than a capacity one — which is why it gets diagnosed late.

Do not depend on public STUN servers in production. Fine for prototypes, but a failed lookup costs you the reflexive candidate and pushes an otherwise-direct call onto relay. Cheap to run, strange to outsource.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "STUN punches a hole through the NAT."

✅ Reality: STUN only reports the address it saw. The hole is punched by your own outbound packet creating a mapping, and whether the peer can use that mapping depends entirely on the NAT's mapping and filtering behaviour. If the mapping is per-destination, no amount of STUN helps — which is precisely when TURN becomes necessary.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "TURN is a fallback, so it barely gets used and does not need planning."

✅ Reality: It carries full media for every session that lands on it, which makes it a bandwidth-bearing service with a capacity plan and usually a significant egress bill. It is a fallback in the ICE priority sense and infrastructure in every operational sense.

❌ Misconception: "ICE picks the fastest path."

✅ Reality: It picks the highest-priority valid pair, and priority is dominated by candidate type. A relayed pair that responded first still loses to a reflexive pair that responded later. Path quality does not enter the formula at all — which is a deliberate simplification, and occasionally the wrong answer.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Quoting a relay-share percentage with no source. Figures around 10–20% circulate widely — including in this vault's own index line — and they vary enormously with user population. The stronger answer names the mechanism (symmetric NAT on both sides forces relay), says you would measure it per network and region, and notes that it drives both the bill and the latency floor.

Conflating STUN and TURN because they share a port and a message format. They are opposite in every operational respect: one stateless and free, one stateful and expensive. Treating them as one service is the fastest way to get the capacity conversation wrong.

Describing NAT types with the old four-name taxonomy. "Full cone, restricted cone, port-restricted, symmetric" is superseded by RFC 4787's two independent axes. The modern vocabulary is more precise and signals current knowledge.

Stopping at "ICE finds a path". The follow-up is which path and why, and the answer is the priority formula's type preferences. Saying "type preference is multiplied by 2^24, so it dominates" is the difference between having read about ICE and having debugged it. The security surface — credentials, quotas, open-relay risk — is the other thing that never comes up unless you raise it.

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency A relayed path is a detour; a badly placed relay can add more delay than the media server. STUN costs one RTT once and nothing after
💰 Cost STUN is negligible. TURN is relay-share × minutes × bitrate, in and out — usually the largest single infrastructure line in a WebRTC product
🔒 Security / visibility Static credentials turn your relay into an open proxy; short-lived per-session credentials and allocation quotas are mandatory, not hardening
📈 Scale TURN is bounded by network interface bandwidth and allocation state, not CPU. It saturates as a quality degradation, not as an error
🔧 Ops complexity Edge placement, anycast or regional selection, credential issuance, and a TLS/443 tier — TURN is four decisions, not a checkbox
🐛 Debuggability getStats() on the nominated candidate pair is the only reliable way to know which path a call took; without it, relay share is unmeasurable

16. Real World Usage

Relay placement is an anycast problem, and Cloudflare wrote it up. Because the relay inserts itself into the media path, the distance from user to relay is added latency for exactly the users already having connectivity trouble. One address with many points of presence removes the client-side region-selection logic that would otherwise be required.

SFU architectures shrink TURN's role, and that is the biggest practical lever. When the peer is a server with a public address rather than another NATed client, the hard case — symmetric NAT on both ends — disappears. Relay is then needed mainly for clients whose egress blocks UDP outright, which is why enterprise-facing products invest in turns: on 443 rather than in more relay capacity. The recurring incident follows from this: one enterprise tightening egress policy moves a slice of sessions onto relay within a day, and the first symptom is a bandwidth graph rather than an alert.

17. Acronym Decoder

ICE — Interactive Connectivity Establishment. Connectivity Establishment is literal: it establishes which of many possible paths actually carries traffic. Interactive refers to the two agents probing cooperatively rather than either one deciding alone — which is why checks must succeed in both directions before a pair is valid.

STUN — Session Traversal Utilities for NAT. Utilities is the honest word: it is not a traversal mechanism, it is a set of small tools, and the one that matters returns the source address the server observed. Decoding it corrects the common belief that STUN does the traversal.

TURN — Traversal Using Relays around NAT. Relays around NAT says exactly what it does: rather than getting through the NAT, it gives both parties a public rendezvous point outside it. The expansion is the mechanism.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)
