  • WebRTC's transport stack (breadth.md) — what runs over the nominated pair once ICE finishes.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • A public server endpoint — when one side has a routable address, the whole problem collapses; this is why client-to-SFU is easy and client-to-client is not.

  • IPv6 end to end (02-ip-packets-routing/10-ip-addressing.md) — removes NAT from the equation entirely, but only when both peers have it.

  • Anycast (02-ip-packets-routing/breadth.md) — the standard way to place relays near users without client-side selection.

  • Egress cost & data transfer pricing (Section 12) — where the TURN bill actually appears.

  • API authentication (Section 10) — short-lived TURN credentials are an ordinary token-issuance problem.

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

The framing is "a user on a corporate network cannot connect — walk me through it", or the design version, "where do you put STUN and TURN for a global product". A strong answer distinguishes the two by cost and state, explains that relay share is driven by user networks rather than your code, places relays at the edge for latency reasons, and notes that an SFU removes most of the need. A weak answer treats TURN as a checkbox in the ICE server list.

Topology diagram

The two client subgraphs are the point: A and B run identical code and take completely different paths, decided entirely by network policy neither you nor they control. B's path costs you relay bandwidth and a TCP transport under real-time media; A's costs you nothing beyond one STUN round trip.

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
10x sessions TURN egress — relay share × concurrent sessions × bitrate, both directions Horizontal relay capacity per region; lower Opus bitrates for audio-only; verify SFU reachability so fewer sessions relay at all
100x Interface saturation per relay, plus allocation state and refresh rate Anycast across more points of presence; separate the turns:443 tier from the UDP tier

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • Relay saturation at 10x, presenting as quality rather than failure. Every client's bandwidth estimation lowers bitrate at once; users report bad audio, connectivity dashboards stay green.

  • Allocation churn at 100x. Refreshes on the 600-second timer become a real request rate, and unclean disconnects hold allocations until expiry.

  • The 3am version: one customer's firewall change. Relay share steps up overnight, the bandwidth graph moves before any alert fires, and nothing in your deploy history explains it.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • Relay share, segmented by region and customer network — the single most valuable WebRTC metric. Predicts cost, predicts latency, changes for reasons outside your control.

  • Nominated candidate-pair type distribution from getStats() — host, reflexive and relayed counts over time. Without it, relay share is a guess.

  • Time-to-connected p50 and p99 — a rising tail means preferred pairs are failing and falling through to relay: a network-policy change, not a code regression.

📚 Reference Links

  • The two behavioural axes — RFC 4787: NAT Behavioral Requirements for Unicast UDP

  • How ICE uses them — RFC 8445 §2: Interactive Connectivity Establishment

  • The clearest prose treatment — WebRTC for the Curious: Connecting

  • Carrier-grade NAT space — RFC 6598: IANA-Reserved IPv4 Prefix for Shared Address Space

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The two independent axes? Mapping behaviour (which external port) and filtering behaviour (who may reply).
What is "symmetric NAT" in modern terms? Address-and-port-dependent mapping — a new port per destination.
When is relay unavoidable? When neither side has endpoint-independent mapping.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Whether two peers can connect directly comes down to two independent NAT behaviours. Mapping decides which external port your NAT uses: endpoint-independent means one port for all destinations, so the address a STUN server reported is the address your peer can use. Address-and-port-dependent — the behaviour people call symmetric — allocates a new port per destination, so the reported address is stale the moment you talk to someone else. Filtering decides who may send back through that mapping. When both sides are per-destination, neither can predict the other's port, and TURN relay is the only remaining option.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why does hole punching work at all, and what exactly makes it fail?

It works because a NAT mapping is created by outbound traffic. When A sends a packet toward B's public address, A's NAT allocates an external port and starts accepting return traffic on it; when B does the same simultaneously, each side's outbound packet opens the door for the other's. Neither side had to receive an unsolicited packet, which is exactly the thing a NAT refuses to forward. ICE's connectivity checks are that mutual send, which is why a pair is only valid when checks succeed in both directions rather than one.

It fails on the two axes independently. If A's NAT uses address-and-port-dependent mapping, the external port it showed the STUN server applies only to the STUN server; the port it uses toward B is different and unpredictable, so B has nothing to aim at. If A's NAT uses address-and-port-dependent filtering, the mapping may be reusable but only traffic from the exact address and port that created it is accepted, so B's packet from a different port is dropped. RFC 4787's requirement that a NAT use endpoint-independent mapping is precisely so this works — and the reason a relay is needed is that plenty of deployed equipment does not comply.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

How much effort is it worth spending to avoid relay?

🎯 Really testing: whether you reach for the architectural fix or keep tuning a peer-to-peer path that cannot be fixed from your side.

Direct-path optimisation has a low ceiling, because the determining behaviour belongs to networks you do not run. You can make gathering complete and prompt — a reachable STUN server, trickle ICE, both IPv4 and IPv6 candidates — and IPv6 genuinely helps, since a peer with a global IPv6 address has no NAT to traverse. Beyond that you are optimising an outcome set by a router in someone else's office.

The high-leverage move is topological. An SFU with a public address converts every session from client-to-client, where two unknown NATs must cooperate, into client-to-server, where only one side is behind NAT. That removes the hard case entirely; what still needs relay is the narrower population whose egress blocks UDP outright, and for those turns: on 443 is the answer. Effort ranking: public endpoint in the path first, TLS/443 second, direct-path tuning as a rounding error.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Mapping behaviour (RFC 4787) Older name Can a peer use the STUN-reported address? Consequence
Endpoint-independent Full cone / restricted cone Yes — one external port for all destinations Direct path likely; STUN is enough
Address-dependent Restricted cone Sometimes — new port per destination address Direct path fragile
Address-and-port-dependent Symmetric No — new port per destination address and port Relay required if the other side is also this
Filtering behaviour Who may send back through the mapping Consequence
Endpoint-independent Anyone Easiest to traverse
Address-dependent Only the address you sent to Hole punching still works after mutual send
Address-and-port-dependent Only the exact address and port Requires precise mutual send; least forgiving

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The trace is the argument. Peer-reflexive discovery gives A a candidate it did not have, which is genuinely useful when B's mapping is endpoint-independent — A simply uses the newly learned port. It fails here because B's NAT allocates per destination, so the port A learned was created for one specific pairing and cannot be reused. That is the mechanical definition of "symmetric NAT breaks P2P", and it is why the failure cannot be worked around from the application.

Two practical corollaries. First, only one side needs endpoint-independent mapping for a direct path to exist — WebRTC for the Curious puts it as "for a call to work, at least one side must be" — which is why a client talking to a public server always works and two clients often do not. Second, mappings expire: RFC 4787 requires a UDP mapping timer of at least two minutes and recommends five or more, which is why WebRTC sends keepalives on an idle media path rather than assuming the hole stays open.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Do not use the old four-name taxonomy in a design discussion. "Full cone, restricted cone, port-restricted cone, symmetric" collapses two independent axes into one list and cannot express the combinations that actually occur. RFC 4787's mapping-and-filtering vocabulary is both more accurate and a signal that the knowledge is current.

Do not try to detect NAT type and branch on it. ICE already probes every pair empirically, which is strictly better than classifying and guessing; the classification is a diagnostic aid for you, not a runtime input. Applications that special-case detected NAT types end up with paths that ICE would have found anyway, plus a code path nobody tests.

Do not assume carrier-grade NAT behaves like a home router. Mobile networks and ISPs using RFC 6598 shared address space put many subscribers behind one address with their own port-allocation policies, and they are disproportionately represented in the population that needs relay. A product with heavy mobile usage should expect a higher relay share than a desktop one.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Symmetric NAT on either end means P2P fails."

✅ Reality: Only if both ends lack endpoint-independent mapping. One cooperative side is enough, because the predictable side can be the target — which is exactly why a client reaching a public server succeeds regardless of the client's NAT.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Hole punching is a trick that defeats the NAT."

✅ Reality: It uses the NAT exactly as designed. Both sides send outbound, each creating the mapping that admits the other's traffic; nothing is bypassed. That is also why it fails cleanly rather than intermittently when the mapping is per-destination — there is no trick to break, just an address that does not exist.

headings.text: 📚 Reference Links
🎯 Recall Check
Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Encryption is mandatory, and this says so — RFC 8827: WebRTC Security Architecture

  • How DTLS keys SRTP — RFC 5764: DTLS Extension to Establish Keys for SRTP

🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The stack, bottom to top? UDP → ICE → DTLS → SRTP for media, SCTP for data.
What does DTLS do for media? Handshakes to derive SRTP keys; it does not carry the media itself.
What is left readable on the wire? RTP headers — sequence number, timestamp, SSRC — authenticated but not encrypted.

Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Everything rides one UDP flow on the ICE-nominated pair. DTLS handshakes over that flow and its exporter produces the SRTP master keys and salts for each direction — so DTLS establishes keys and then steps aside, while SRTP does the per-packet work on the media. Data channels take the other branch: SCTP encapsulated in that same DTLS association, sharing the port with media. RFC 8827 makes this non-negotiable — all media must use SRTP, plaintext RTP is forbidden, and all data channels must run over DTLS. There is no unencrypted mode to fall into.

Where it matters: it explains what you can and cannot see when debugging. SRTP encrypts the payload but leaves the RTP header readable and authenticated, so a capture still shows you sequence numbers, timestamps and SSRCs — enough to diagnose loss and reordering without decrypting anything. It also explains why a single failed DTLS handshake kills both media and data at once: they share one association. (→ ICE, STUN & TURN · SDP offer/answer, for a=fingerprint and a=setup)

headings.text: 📚 Reference Links
🎯 Recall Check

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The protocol — RFC 8831: WebRTC Data Channels

  • The API surface — MDN: RTCDataChannel

🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What transport? SCTP encapsulated in DTLS, over the same ICE-negotiated UDP flow as media.
The two reliability knobs? maxRetransmits or maxPacketLifeTime — one or the other, never both.
The independent third option? ordered, default true.

Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A data channel carries arbitrary bytes between peers over SCTP inside the DTLS association the media already established. Its distinguishing feature is tunable reliability: RFC 8831 supports fully reliable delivery and partially reliable delivery via PR-SCTP, with ordering independently switchable. Setting maxRetransmits: 0 with ordered: false gives UDP-like behaviour — each message sent once, delivered or not, in whatever order arrives — which is exactly right for state that the next update supersedes. Full reliability with ordering behaves like a stream and suits file transfer.

Where it matters: the useful framing is that a data channel is a free side effect of a peer connection you already needed, not a reason to create one. Cursor positions, game state, control messages and telemetry between two clients avoid a server round trip entirely. But standing up signaling, STUN, TURN and ICE purely to move JSON to your own backend is inverted engineering — that is a WebSocket. (→ The three WebRTC APIs · WebRTC vs WebSocket for audio)

notes.title: Topologies — Mesh vs SFU vs MCU

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification
What does an SFU actually do to the packets, and why is that cheap?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
At what point do you introduce a media server, and would you ever mix modes?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The three topologies compared — WebRTC for the Curious: Applied WebRTC

  • An SFU as a library rather than a server — mediasoup: Design

  • A managed SFU plus agent framework — LiveKit documentation

  • RTP usage the forwarder has to respect — RFC 8834: Media Transport and Use of RTP in WebRTC

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Client uplink in a mesh of n? n-1 encodes and uploads per client — quadratic across the session.
What does an SFU do that an MCU does not? Forwards streams unmodified; no decode, no re-encode.
Why does an MCU cost so much? It decodes and re-encodes every stream into a composite.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Three ways to get media between more than two people. Mesh connects everyone directly, so each client encodes and uploads its stream once per other participant — simple, no server, and it collapses around four or five people on real uplinks. An SFU takes one upload per client and forwards the packets it selects to each receiver without touching them, which keeps server CPU low and scales linearly. An MCU decodes everything, composites one output stream and re-encodes it, which is expensive but gives every client a single stream to decode. Practically everything modern is an SFU.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

What does an SFU actually do to the packets, and why is that cheap?

Almost nothing, which is the point. It terminates ICE, DTLS and SRTP with each participant separately — so it does decrypt and re-encrypt at the packet level — but it does not decode the media. It reads RTP headers, decides which streams each receiver should get, rewrites sequence numbers and timestamps to keep each outgoing stream coherent, and forwards. No codec runs, so the cost per stream is packet handling and bandwidth rather than CPU, and a single machine can carry far more participants than an MCU on the same hardware.

That design also explains the SFU's characteristic features. Because it forwards rather than mixes, each receiver can be sent a different subset — active speakers only, or a lower-quality layer for a small tile — which is what simulcast and SVC exist to enable: the sender publishes several encodings and the SFU picks per receiver. And because it terminates SRTP, media is encrypted client-to-SFU rather than client-to-client, which is why "end-to-end encrypted" needs qualifying in any SFU product unless a separate insertable-streams layer is in place.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

At what point do you introduce a media server, and would you ever mix modes?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard second release of any product that shipped 1:1 calling first.

The arithmetic says mesh survives to about three or four participants on typical residential uplinks, since each client uploads n-1 copies of its own stream while decoding n-1 incoming. Audio-only stretches further because Opus at conversational bitrates is cheap, but encode and connection overhead still grows per peer. So the mechanical trigger is small, and for video it arrives almost immediately.

The more interesting question is whether to run mesh for two and switch at three, and my answer is usually no. Mode switching means two media paths with different failure modes, two recording stories, two sets of statistics, and a transition that fires exactly when a call is becoming more important. It also does not survive server-side consumers: recording, transcription, moderation and any AI agent all need the media to reach a server, and once that is true for one feature it is true for every session.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Mesh SFU MCU When you'd actually pick it
Client uplink n-1 streams 1 stream 1 stream SFU and MCU both fix the client-side quadratic
Client downlink n-1 n-1 (selectable) 1 composite MCU wins for very weak receivers
Server CPU None Low — packet forwarding High — decode + re-encode MCU cost is per room, not per packet
Server bandwidth None n in, n(n-1) out n in, n out MCU is cheapest in bandwidth, dearest in CPU
Layout control Client-side Client-side Server-side, fixed MCU when you need one fixed rendering
Encryption Client to client Client to SFU Client to MCU Only mesh is genuinely end-to-end by default
Pick when 2 participants, no server consumer Anything else Legacy interop, very constrained clients SFU is the default in 2026

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The arithmetic is the decision. For n participants: mesh holds n(n-1)/2 connections with each client sending n-1 streams and receiving n-1. An SFU takes n streams in and sends n(n-1) out, so the quadratic moves from the weakest client to a server you can size — and server egress becomes the dominant cost. An MCU takes n in and sends n out, the cheapest bandwidth profile of the three, paid for with a decode and encode per stream per room.

Simulcast is what makes the SFU's downlink tractable. A sender publishes the same video at two or three qualities and the SFU picks per receiver, based on that receiver's estimated bandwidth and how the stream is displayed. Without it one quality goes to everyone, so the weakest receiver dictates quality for all or drops packets — mesh's failure, relocated. It is also why SFU products care so much about bandwidth estimation: the forwarding decision is only as good as the estimate feeding it.

Server-side composition is not exclusively an MCU. Recording, streaming to a CDN and feeding a model one mixed audio track are MCU-shaped operations that modern systems run as a separate pipeline beside the SFU rather than as the topology for live participants — pay the decode cost once for the consumer that needs it, keep forwarding for everyone else.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Do not choose an MCU for general conferencing. The per-stream decode and re-encode cost is high, it adds a full transcode of latency, and it removes the receiver's ability to choose quality or layout. Its remaining niches are legacy interop and receivers too constrained to decode multiple streams.

Do not treat an SFU as stateless infrastructure. It holds per-participant transport, keys and subscription state, so routing must be affinity-aware, deploys must drain rather than restart, and a room cannot be load-balanced across instances without an inter-server forwarding layer. Sizing it like a web tier is the standard mistake.

Do not claim end-to-end encryption on an SFU path without qualification. The SFU terminates SRTP; it can see the media. Genuine end-to-end encryption through a forwarder requires an additional layer such as insertable streams, and it costs you the SFU's ability to make quality decisions on content it can no longer inspect.

Do not build mesh past a demo. It is the right answer for exactly two participants and a tempting answer for three, and the failure it produces — the weakest participant's uplink degrading everyone else's experience — is the one users cannot diagnose or report accurately.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "An SFU is just a relay, so it is like TURN."

✅ Reality: TURN forwards opaque packets between two endpoints with no knowledge of what they are. An SFU terminates SRTP per participant, reads RTP headers, rewrites sequence numbers, and selects which streams and which simulcast layer each receiver gets. It is a media-aware participant, which is why it can do quality adaptation and TURN cannot.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Mesh scales fine for small groups because there is no server bottleneck."

✅ Reality: The bottleneck moved to the participant with the worst uplink, which is worse — you cannot provision it, you cannot see it, and its degradation shows up in everyone else's experience rather than in the affected user's. "No server" means "no capacity you control".

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • ICE, STUN & TURN (81-ice-stun-turn.md) — an SFU's public address is what removes most of the traversal problem.

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • WebRTC for voice AI (87-webrtc-for-voice-ai.md) — the agent is a participant on the SFU, which is why the topology decision comes first.

  • Media pipeline basics (breadth.md) — simulcast and bandwidth estimation, which the SFU's forwarding decision depends on.

  • Sticky sessions / session affinity and Load balancing algorithms (Section 11) — routing participants to a stateful media server.

📚 Reference Links

  • The audio codec you will actually ship — RFC 6716 §2: Definition of the Opus Audio Codec

  • RTCP feedback, NACK/PLI and bandwidth estimation — WebRTC for the Curious: Media Communication

🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Opus frame sizes and bitrate range? 2.5–60 ms frames (20 ms typical); 6–510 kbit/s.
What does the jitter buffer trade? Latency for smoothness — and it grows adaptively on a lossy path.
The bandwidth-estimation acronyms? GCC, with REMB and TWCC as the feedback mechanisms.

Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Between the microphone and the far speaker sits a pipeline worth being able to name. Opus encodes audio in 2.5–60 ms frames across 6–510 kbit/s, with speech comfortable in the teens; video uses VP8, VP9, H.264 or AV1, where the intra-frame versus inter-frame distinction explains why a lost keyframe is catastrophic and a lost delta frame is not. The receiver's jitter buffer holds packets to absorb arrival variance, trading latency for smoothness. RTCP carries the feedback loop — NACK for selective retransmission, PLI to demand a fresh keyframe, and REMB or TWCC feeding Google Congestion Control, which tells the encoder what bitrate the path will actually bear.

Where it matters: the jitter buffer is adaptive, so a lossy path silently spends latency budget you thought you had — which is why an end-to-end mouth-to-ear measurement beats reasoning from component numbers. Simulcast is the other term to know: a sender publishes several encodings so an SFU can forward a different quality to each receiver, without which the weakest receiver dictates quality for everyone. (→ Topologies — mesh vs SFU vs MCU · WebRTC for voice AI)

notes.title: WebRTC for Voice AI

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification
Walk me through the latency budget from speech to first audible response.
Tier 2 — Trade-off
The provider offers both WebRTC and WebSocket. Which do you use where, and why?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • A provider's own WebRTC path, including the ephemeral-key model — OpenAI: Realtime API with WebRTC

  • The agent-beside-the-SFU pattern — LiveKit documentation

  • The codec's contribution to the budget — RFC 6716 §2: Definition of the Opus Audio Codec

  • Why relay placement is a latency decision — Cloudflare: TURN and anycast — making peer connections work globally

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Why WebRTC rather than a WebSocket from a browser? Loss concealment and congestion control on hostile last-mile networks.
Where does the agent sit? As another participant on the SFU — not as a special path.
Which credential model does a browser client use? A short-lived ephemeral key minted by your backend, never a real API key.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A realtime voice agent is a latency budget with a model in the middle. The standard shape is browser to a nearby edge over WebRTC, into an SFU or gateway, and from there to a worker running speech recognition, the model and speech synthesis, publishing the reply back into the session as an ordinary audio track. WebRTC is used at the client edge specifically because last-mile networks lose packets and a TCP-based transport stalls on them; inside the data centre a WebSocket is fine. The whole design question is which hops you can remove, because every one of them spends budget you cannot get back later.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Walk me through the latency budget from speech to first audible response.

The terms are additive and there are more than people expect. Capture and encode contribute Opus frame time — 20 ms typically, from a 2.5–60 ms range — plus algorithmic delay that RFC 6716 places between 5 and 65.2 ms depending on configuration. Transit to the edge is whatever the user's path costs, doubled if the session is relayed through TURN. The receiving jitter buffer is adaptive, so a lossy path silently grows it; on a bad connection it is frequently the largest single term you nominally control.

Then the part that is not networking: endpointing — deciding the user has stopped speaking — plus recognition, inference to first token, and synthesis to first audio frame. Endpointing deserves naming because it is often the biggest contributor and it is a tuning decision rather than a physical constraint; waiting longer for silence makes the agent feel slower but reduces false interruptions. The reason to enumerate all of it is that transport and hop count are the terms you can still buy back after the model is chosen, and they are usually worth a few hundred milliseconds.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

The provider offers both WebRTC and WebSocket. Which do you use where, and why?

🎯 Really testing: whether you pick by network conditions rather than by convenience — the WebSocket path is easier and is the right answer in exactly one place.

Use WebRTC where the network is hostile and WebSocket where it is not, which in practice means WebRTC from browsers and mobile clients, WebSocket from your own servers. OpenAI's Realtime API documentation makes exactly this split, recommending WebRTC for browser and mobile clients for latency consistency and positioning WebSocket for server-side connections. The mechanism behind the recommendation is that audio over a TCP-framed transport head-of-line blocks on loss: one missing segment delays every subsequent frame, producing a stall rather than a brief artefact, and real-time audio would much rather conceal a lost packet than wait for it.

The second consideration is what the browser gives you free on the WebRTC path — echo cancellation, noise suppression, gain control, jitter buffering, congestion control and device handling. Over a raw WebSocket you ship all of that yourself or accept an agent that hears its own speaker output. Inside a data centre none of it matters, and a WebSocket is simpler to operate, authenticate and debug. That is the whole rule: WebRTC at the edge, WebSocket in the core.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Hop Transport Why What it costs you
Browser / mobile → edge WebRTC Loss concealment, congestion control, built-in audio processing ICE, TURN, an SFU or gateway to operate
Edge SFU → agent worker WebSocket or gRPC Reliable, short, inside your network A hop — keep it in-region
Agent worker → model provider WebSocket (server-side) Simpler auth and observability; loss is not the problem here Provider round trip, unavoidable
Agent worker → session WebRTC publish The reply is just another participant's track Nothing extra — reuses the session
Telephony ingress SIP → gateway → WebRTC Meets the PSTN where it is A transcode and a gateway to run

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The budget is a sum, and hop count is the term you control. Everything in that sequence adds: frame time and codec delay at capture, transit to the edge, forwarding, the endpointing decision, the provider round trip, synthesis to first frame, transit back, jitter buffer. Nothing parallelises except starting synthesis before the model finishes generating — which is why streaming token output into a streaming synthesiser is the highest-leverage optimisation in the path: it changes the shape of the sum rather than one of its terms.

Barge-in is what makes this architecture rather than plumbing. The user must be able to interrupt, so the inbound path stays open while the agent speaks and the agent must cancel synthesis and discard queued audio within a frame or two. A strictly turn-based design demos fine and feels broken in conversation. It also constrains echo handling: the agent's own output must not be transcribed as user speech, which is precisely what the browser's echo cancellation does on the WebRTC path.

Placement follows from the sum — edge near the user, worker near the edge, provider connection from a region close to both. A relayed session adds its detour twice, so relay placement matters more here than in a conferencing product, because a voice agent has no slack to absorb it.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Do not put WebRTC between your own services. Inside the data centre, loss is not the problem WebRTC solves, and you have taken on ICE, DTLS and per-session state for nothing. The provider guidance is explicit that server-side connections should use WebSocket.

Do not ship a real API key to the browser. The ephemeral-key pattern exists because the browser talks directly to the provider after setup: your backend mints a short-lived token, the browser uses that. A long-lived key in client JavaScript is a billing incident waiting to be discovered.

Do not treat this as a streaming-text problem with audio attached. The hard parts are endpointing, barge-in, echo handling and the jitter buffer — none of which appear in a text-streaming architecture, and all of which decide whether the agent feels conversational.

Do not optimise transport before measuring the split. If endpointing is waiting 700 ms for silence, shaving a network hop is noise. Measure the budget by phase first; the term to attack is usually not the one that was easiest to notice.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Audio over WebSocket is fine — it is the same bytes."

✅ Reality: It is the same bytes over a transport that guarantees ordering, so one lost segment stalls every frame behind it. Real-time audio prefers to conceal a loss and move on. On a clean network the difference is invisible; on a phone with two bars it is the whole experience, which is why the provider recommendation is specifically about client networks.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "The model's latency dominates, so transport hardly matters."

✅ Reality: Transport, hop count, jitter buffering and endpointing routinely account for several hundred milliseconds, and unlike the model they are still yours to fix after the architecture is chosen. Teams that shipped audio over a WebSocket to a distant region usually find their largest single win there.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • Time-to-first-token as a network problem and Long-lived connections at scale (Section 16) — the same budget arithmetic for text streaming.

  • Streaming LLM tokens (Section 16) — streaming synthesis is the audio analogue, and the reason the sum changes shape.

  • Tail latency (Section 14) — p99 is what a conversation actually feels, not p50.

notes.title: WebRTC vs WebSocket for Audio

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification
What actually happens to audio over a WebSocket when the network drops packets?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
So when is a WebSocket the right call for audio, and what do you have to build?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The provider's own client-versus-server split — OpenAI: Realtime API with WebRTC

  • What the codec contributes either way — RFC 6716 §2: Definition of the Opus Audio Codec

  • Loss handling WebRTC gives you — WebRTC for the Curious: Media Communication

  • Capture, and the processing that comes with it — MDN: MediaDevices.getUserMedia()

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The one mechanical difference that decides it? TCP head-of-line blocking under loss versus UDP loss concealment.
What do you lose by leaving WebRTC? Echo cancellation, noise suppression, AGC, jitter buffer, congestion control.
Where is raw audio over WebSocket clearly right? Server-to-server, and any path where loss is negligible.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Both move audio bidirectionally with sub-second latency, so the choice is not about capability. WebSocket runs on TCP, which guarantees ordering — meaning one lost segment delays every frame behind it, so loss becomes a stall rather than a brief artefact. WebRTC runs on UDP and is built to conceal loss instead of waiting for it, and it brings echo cancellation, noise suppression, jitter buffering and congestion control with it. On a clean network you cannot tell them apart; on a phone with two bars, that difference is the entire experience. So the rule is WebRTC where the network is hostile, WebSocket where it is not.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

What actually happens to audio over a WebSocket when the network drops packets?

TCP retransmits, and the receiving stack will not deliver bytes out of order, so every frame queued behind the missing segment waits for the retransmission. For a file that is exactly right. For live audio it is the wrong trade: a 20 ms frame that arrives 300 ms late is worthless, because the moment it belonged to has passed, and meanwhile 15 perfectly good frames sat in a buffer waiting for it. The user hears a gap and then a burst, or the application's own buffer grows to absorb it and the conversation drifts further behind real time with every loss event.

WebRTC inverts the priority. Media rides SRTP over UDP, so a lost packet is simply missing; the decoder conceals it — repeating or interpolating a frame's worth of audio — and playback stays aligned with real time. Selective retransmission exists for cases where it can arrive in time, and forward error correction can carry redundancy for exactly this reason, but nothing blocks. The jitter buffer absorbs arrival variance rather than absorbing retransmission delay, which is a much smaller and more predictable job.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

So when is a WebSocket the right call for audio, and what do you have to build?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can defend the simpler option rather than reflexively reaching for the heavier stack.

A WebSocket is right whenever the path is reliable and operational simplicity is worth something — server-to-server audio, connections inside a data centre or region, and prototypes where getting the model responding matters more than the last hundred milliseconds. One connection, ordinary auth, ordinary observability, no ICE, no TURN, no per-session media state. Providers draw the same line from the other side: OpenAI recommends WebRTC for browser and mobile clients and positions WebSocket for server-side connections.

What you take on using it from a browser is the audio pipeline. getUserMedia still gives you capture with echo cancellation, noise suppression and gain control on the track, but once you pull raw PCM through an audio worklet and frame it yourself you own encoding, packetisation, a jitter buffer, silence handling, reconnect-with-resume, and the decision about what to do when the socket stalls. That is real code WebRTC would have provided, and the honest test is whether your users' networks are good enough that you never write the hard parts. For an internal tool on wired corporate networks, often yes. For a consumer mobile product, no.

4. Quick Comparison Table

WebRTC Raw audio over WebSocket When the difference decides
Transport UDP (SRTP/DTLS), TCP only via TURN fallback TCP Lossy last-mile networks
Loss behaviour Conceal, selective retransmit, FEC Head-of-line blocking The single most important row
Jitter buffer Built in and adaptive You build it Owning a jitter buffer is real work
Echo cancellation / noise suppression / AGC Built in Track-level only; pipeline is yours Agent hears its own output otherwise
Congestion control Built in, media-aware TCP's, which is not media-aware Bitrate adaptation on a degrading link
Setup cost ICE, STUN, TURN, signaling One connection Prototypes and server-side paths
Ops surface Four services One The honest reason teams pick WebSocket
Pick when Browser or mobile client, hostile network Server-to-server, in-region, reliable path —

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The arithmetic is what a late frame is worth. With 20 ms Opus frames, recovering a lost frame costs at least one round trip; on a 60 ms path that is 60 ms during which three more frames have arrived and are being withheld. The receiver either stalls or grows its buffer, and a buffer that grows never shrinks quickly — so each loss event permanently pushes the conversation further behind real time. Concealment costs one frame of degraded audio and nothing else.

What you give up leaving WebRTC is a pipeline, not a protocol. The browser's capture stack applies echo cancellation, noise suppression and gain control; WebRTC adds encode, packetisation, an adaptive jitter buffer, loss concealment, selective retransmission, FEC and bandwidth estimation feeding back into the encoder. A WebSocket implementation gets the first group free from getUserMedia and must build or forgo the second. Echo is the one to name: without cancellation on a speaker-and-microphone device the agent transcribes its own voice, which is immediately obvious to anyone who has tried it.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Do not choose WebRTC for a server-to-server audio hop. Loss inside a data centre is negligible, so the mechanism that justifies WebRTC does not apply, and you have taken on ICE, DTLS and per-session state for no benefit.

Do not choose a WebSocket for a consumer mobile client. Mobile last-mile loss is exactly the condition TCP handles worst for real-time media, and the degradation is a stall — the failure mode users describe as "it froze", not "it sounded rough".

Do not benchmark this on your office wired connection. The two transports are indistinguishable on a clean path, which is precisely why the WebSocket prototype always looks fine. Test under simulated loss — a few percent, with jitter — or you have measured nothing relevant to the decision.

Do not forget that TURN over TCP puts you back in the same place. A WebRTC session relayed over turns: on 443 has TCP underneath the media and inherits head-of-line blocking. That is still the right fallback, but it means "we use WebRTC" is not by itself a guarantee about loss behaviour for every session.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "WebSocket is real-time, so it is fine for real-time audio."

✅ Reality: It is low-latency when nothing is lost, which is a different property. Real-time media needs the transport to give up on late data, and TCP is architecturally incapable of that. "Real-time" describes the latency target; the question is what happens when the target is missed.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "The difference is only about latency numbers, so a few tens of milliseconds either way."

✅ Reality: It is about behaviour under loss, and the gap is not a constant — it is zero on a good network and unbounded on a bad one. That is why the honest comparison is a distribution rather than an average, and why p99 is the number that decides.
